title: Rethinking KYC
gist: a16z Crypto argues KYC is not the blocker to institutions onchain: BSA obligations attach to an institution's own customers, not the settlement network, and reusable credentials, ZK proofs, KYW/KYA/KYT tooling and token-level controls can cut redundant checks. Extends to Know Your Agent for AI agent payments.

themes.theme: Legal baseline: who must be identified

insights.claim: A bank's BSA customer-identification obligations apply to the customers who open accounts with it, not to every participant in the underlying settlement infrastructure, so settling on a permissionless chain or trading against a liquidity pool does not make counterparties the bank's customers.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Removes a key perceived legal barrier to TradFi institutions using public blockchains; supports tokenization adoption.

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act places AML and sanctions obligations on the permitted stablecoin issuer, the identifiable application-layer entity, rather than on the permissionless networks its stablecoins circulate on.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Congress has already endorsed issuer-level, not network-level, compliance allocation; supportive for stablecoin issuers on public chains.
insights.locator: The good news is that new, affirmative legislation

insights.claim: No new US legislation is needed to enable crypto-native KYC; existing law can be adapted through interpretive guidance, rulemaking, or innovation exemptions.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Regulatory change can come fast via agency guidance; watch FinCEN/banking-agency FAQs and exemptions.
insights.locator: The good news is that new, affirmative legislation

insights.claim: FinCEN's April 2026 proposal named machine learning, GenAI, digital identity, blockchain analytics and APIs as innovative AML/CFT approaches and said institutions that responsibly experiment will not incur additional supervisory risk solely for using them.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Regulatory tailwind for compliance-tech and onchain analytics vendors.
insights.quote: institutions that “responsibly experiment with innovative technologies in their AML/CFT programs will not incur any additional risk

insights.claim: September 2026 interagency FAQs expressly recognize that qualifying verifiable digital credentials can be used within a bank's Customer Identification Program, though they do not approve every decentralized identifier or credential design.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: First formal opening for verifiable credentials in bank KYC; beneficiaries are credential issuers and wallet-identity providers with compliant designs.
insights.locator: Verifiable credentials could support or replace

themes.theme: Redundant KYC and the reuse problem

insights.claim: Institutions do not want to avoid KYC but to avoid redundant KYC, which is costly for platforms, adds user friction and is increasingly unreliable as deepfake tools proliferate.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Reusable KYC is a cost-saving wedge; deepfakes erode the value of repeated document/selfie checks.
insights.quote: Institutions do not want to avoid KYC; they want to avoid redundant KYC.
insights.locator: Reusability and the ecosystem of trust

insights.claim: SWIFT's KYC Registry, launched in 2014, spans nearly 8,000 institutions across 200+ countries and works because relationships are institution-to-institution with known counterparties; crypto has no equivalent centralized registry.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Shows reusable KYC scales when counterparties are known; the crypto equivalent is an open commercial opportunity.
insights.locator: A useful analog in traditional financial markets

insights.claim: Centralized identity PII stores act as honeypots for criminals, and a mobile ID discloses full name, address, date of birth and photo in one disclosure, which is why privacy advocates urge alternatives to repeated government-ID submission.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Privacy-preserving verification (selective disclosure, ZK) has a security as well as a compliance case.

insights.claim: Large KYC providers can build single-sign-on-style trust networks, with basic verification costing roughly $1 to $2 charged to the originating platform and secondary platforms needing only partial KYC such as a liveness check; examples include Sumsub ID, World ID, MoonPay and Stripe via Privy.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Unit economics of reusable KYC are cheap; incumbents with large verified user bases hold the distribution advantage.

insights.claim: Access to pools of pre-verified users (whitelisted liquidity) is a form of compliance distribution, not a legal requirement, and an institution's own obligations are the same in a gated or permissionless pool.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Against the common view that institutions must use permissioned venues; permissionless DeFi access may be legally viable.

insights.claim: Issuers are seeking introductions to global exchanges to leverage their compliance frameworks, but the commercial structure for such distribution is still being developed.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Partnering with compliant exchanges is the simplest near-term route to customers; commercial terms are not yet settled.

themes.theme: Reliance vs outsourcing and legal frictions

insights.claim: Under BSA customer-identification rules, reliance is a legal safe harbor applying only when relying on another regulated financial institution; using non-qualifying vendors such as identity-verification firms or credit bureaus is outsourcing, leaving the institution fully responsible for CIP.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Reusable-KYC products that lack a regulated-institution issuer do not shift liability; diligence the legal basis before relying on them.

insights.claim: FATF's third-party reliance conditions (third party regulated and supervised, immediate access to underlying KYC data, relying institution retains liability) conflict with the privacy-preserving design of most onchain KYC, since PII must be producible on demand.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Structural tension between privacy tech and AML rules; solutions will need a trusted source of record somewhere.
insights.locator: This doesn’t always neatly map to crypto.

insights.claim: Many crypto platforms, even registered money services businesses or state-chartered trust companies, are not regulated institutions for purposes of the federal AML/CIP reliance rule and so cannot be counterparties to formal reliance, though this is evolving as more crypto firms become licensed.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Licensing status determines whether crypto firms can supply KYC others may legally rely on.

insights.claim: The US Travel Rule applies to transfers above roughly $3,000 between financial institutions and VASPs but does not require data to go to self-hosted wallets, so institutions need not lose sleep over Travel Rule compliance with DeFi or self-hosted wallets, though non-US jurisdictions may differ.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: US exposure to DeFi is less constrained by the Travel Rule than often assumed; cross-border regimes may be stricter.
insights.locator: In addition to AML program requirements

insights.claim: Not every KYC determination reduces to a binary cryptographic proof: proofs can confirm birth date, citizenship, sanctions-check results or credential possession, but judgment-intensive AML inquiries still need traditional diligence.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Credentials replace components of CIP, not risk-based due diligence; do not expect full automation.

insights.claim: Soulbound-style nontransferable tokens can record KYC results on a wallet, but nontransferability alone does not stop someone else taking control of the wallet, so systems need expiration and revocation (Quadrata supports issuer-controlled revocation).
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Evaluate onchain identity products on revocation and wallet-binding, not just token issuance.

insights.claim: Burrata tried to issue onchain identity tokens and, while technically viable, was unable to find product-market fit and shut down.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Technical feasibility of onchain identity has not guaranteed demand; distribution matters more than primitives.
insights.quote: unable to find product market fit

insights.claim: Zero-knowledge passport proofs (Self.xyz pre-KYC, Aztec-owned zkPassport) let users prove attributes such as being over 18 or not sanctioned without revealing data, useful as a gating layer before formal KYC to screen out bots and sanctioned wallets.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: ZK pre-KYC reduces onboarding cost but does not replace formal CIP.

insights.claim: Proof-of-personhood systems such as World ID (iris biometrics via the Orb) and Human Passport address Sybil attacks and deepfakes by proving a unique human, not regulatory identity, so must be combined with other KYC approaches.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Personhood is a complement to KYC; relevant to deepfake-driven fraud and bot resistance.
insights.quote: Note that proof of personhood addresses issues like Sybil attacks and deepfakes

insights.claim: Privado ID, SpruceID and Fireblocks Open Transaction Layer are pursuing portable KYC via verifiable credentials or shared protocols, with Fireblocks' OTL leaving KYC to existing regulated entities in the network.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Several competing standards; winners will likely be those distributed through incumbents holding KYC'd user bases.
insights.locator: One recent example is the Fireblocks Open Transaction Layer

insights.claim: RWA issuers embed transfer restrictions in the token contract itself: Securitize's BlackRock BUIDL and Apollo ACRED, Ondo's OUSG and Superstate's USTB only permit transfers between allowlisted, verified wallets.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Token-level compliance lets tokenized funds settle on public chains; this is the dominant design for institutional tokenized treasuries.

insights.claim: Asset provenance degrades as tokens cross bridges, get wrapped or serve as DeFi collateral, but OFAC does not treat an institution as inheriting sanctions status from every address an asset passed through; attenuated multi-hop exposure is managed with risk thresholds, quarantine and SARs.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Operational, not liability, risk; blockchain analytics vendors benefit from threshold-based exposure management.
insights.locator: The unresolved question in KYA is provenance

insights.claim: Neither the BSA nor sanctions law requires permissioned validators or network-wide access controls; institutions may choose designs such as Canton (public permissioned) or Circle's Arc (public chain, KYC'd validators) provided they meet their own obligations.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Institutional chain choice is a product decision, not a legal mandate; supports permissionless L1/L2 competitiveness.

insights.claim: Permissionless protocols are adding gating primitives: Solana token-extension transfer hooks, Uniswap v4 hooks for permissioned pools, Hyperliquid HIP-3 deployer restrictions, and Morpho vaults and kyc-gated markets, while a third party's gated pool does not make the protocol permissioned.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: DeFi venues can host institutional flow without becoming permissioned; watch Morpho and Uniswap v4 as institutional on-ramps.
insights.locator: Some permissionless protocols also offer features

insights.claim: LayerZero (OFT standard, configurable DVNs) and Chainlink (Automated Compliance Engine, CrossChain Identifier) propagate compliance state across chains so KYC, sanctions screening and Travel Rule checks need not be rebuilt per chain.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Crosschain compliance infrastructure is an emerging moat for interoperability protocols.

insights.claim: As AI agents transact onchain and make payments, institutions will need credentials attesting who authorized an agent, on whose behalf and within what constraints; without that, liability for agent actions is effectively nobody and everybody.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Agent identity and authorization is a new compliance layer; early standards and vendors may capture it.
insights.quote: the untenable and uncomfortable “nobody and everybody.”

insights.claim: ERC-8004, deployed to Ethereum mainnet in January 2026, is an early agent-identity standard that attracted more than 30,000 registrations in its first week, and Self Agent ID binds agents to passport-verified human proofs.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Strong early registration suggests demand for onchain agent registries; monitor adoption beyond registrations.

insights.claim: Payments incumbents and crypto firms are building offchain agent frameworks using signed mandates, JWTs and RFC 9421 signatures, including Google AP2, Catena Labs ACK, Skyfire KYAPay, Circle Agent Wallets, Anchorage, Mastercard Agent Pay, Visa Intelligent Commerce, Zero Hash and Ledger.
insights.speaker: Maggie Hsu
insights.so_what: Agentic commerce rails are a crowded race between card networks, custodians and crypto-native players; watch for interoperability standards.
